turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on in, I'll grab vitals while he finishes the last chart. Blood pressure is one thirty-two over eighty-four.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that okay? I don't know, doctor — wait, you're the nurse. Sorry.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Nurse, yep. Pulse is sixty-two, temp thirty-six point six Celsius, oxygen sat ninety-eight percent. All fine for now. He'll be right in.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thanks for letting me stay. I'm her husband. She's been running on empty.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): One sec. This is not your chart, of course it isn't. Okay, there you are. What's going on?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. I'm tired. Like, tired tired. And I'm cold all the time. I figured it's work, and I'm fifty-two, so, you know.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cold all the time. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. My mom had a thyroid problem. That's the whole reason he dragged me here.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? The screen just flashed. Your mom?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother. She took thyroid pills for years. I don't know which ones.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright. Back to you, though. The cold feeling — how long?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, months. Five-ish months? Maybe longer. I don't know.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Longer. It was going on last winter, before the holidays. Closer to a year.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think a whole year. I really don't know, doctor.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you two are between about five months and a year. I'm not going to make you settle it.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She also put on weight. Won't buy new pants.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Weight up? How much are we talking?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten or twelve pounds, I think. I haven't been eating more. Work's just insane, I'm there late.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Since last spring she went from a size eight to a twelve. That's not ten pounds.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay. What about your bowels, any constipation?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): The office is freezing, that's what I was saying. Sweater in July, space heater under the desk.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): I got that part. I asked about bowels. Constipation or no?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Yeah. I'm constipated. Every three days, sometimes four. For a couple months.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mood. How's that been?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Low, I guess. I don't cry. I just don't care about stuff. I blamed turning fifty-two and the job.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She snaps, then she feels awful. She's not like that.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hang on, what was that? I was clicking the wrong tab.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Short temper, then guilty. Not herself.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sleep?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep a ton. Nine, ten hours and I'm still wiped out. I don't know if that's bad.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Skin or hair changing?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Skin's dry, yeah. Hair, I don't know, doctor. Maybe. I'm not sure.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Periods still regular?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): They stopped. I had a hysterectomy. Four years ago? Five-ish. Fibroids.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you actually taking?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, a multivitamin. And vitamin D, two thousand units, once a day. I think that's all. Wait, is coffee a medicine? No, never mind.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The antidepressant. Tell her about that.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Sertraline. I stopped it.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Dose? And when did you stop? Sorry, say the dose again, someone knocked in my headset and there's no one there.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I think fifty milligrams? I don't know, doctor. I stopped it in March. It made me flat. Or I was already flat.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anyone ever put you on thyroid hormone? Levothyroxine, Synthroid, any of those?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): They wrote it once, years back, and I never filled it. Never took one pill.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good to know. And that old thyroid test — what did they tell you?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Borderline, they said. I don't know when. Two years, maybe more. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0045] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not right. Maple Street clinic, you came home and said normal. You keep remembering borderline and it's wrong.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I remember borderline. Maybe I made that up. I don't know.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm trying to open the outside records. This computer is molasses. Clinic name again?
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Maple Street. Three years ago, I want to say. In the fall.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nothing in here. I can't tell if it was borderline or normal, or if we even have it.
[SEG0050] person_1 (NURSE): Knock knock. You want labs today, or is she coming back fasting? I've got a chair open.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm going to start a low dose of levothyroxine, twenty-five micrograms daily, and we'll just get a TSH next week.
[SEG0052] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She never took the last one. You're starting a pill with no new blood test?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. I'd rather not, if we don't actually know. My mom's dose was always getting changed.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yeah, you're right. Forget the prescription — no levothyroxine today. New plan. Bloodwork before you leave: TSH, free T4, and a CBC. Not fasting.
[SEG0055] person_1 (NURSE): I'll set the tubes up. Allergies? I ask everybody, even for a simple draw.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. I don't think so.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sulfa. Your lip blew up that one time, remember?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): That was ages ago and I don't even know if it was the sulfa. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll mark a possible sulfa reaction with lip swelling, and that the two of you don't agree. Nothing we're doing today involves sulfa.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay.

[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me read this back, if the screen will let me. Vitamin D two thousand units daily, a multivitamin, sertraline stopped, thyroid hormone never taken. Are you actually taking the vitamin D every day?
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days. I forget weekends. I don't know how many I skip.
[SEG0063] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's more than weekends.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright, adherence is a guess. Keep taking it anyway. And do not start a thyroid pill on your own while we wait.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it my thyroid?
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): My working thought is an underactive thyroid. Not a diagnosis. The job and just getting older could explain pieces of it, so I'm not locking it in.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Should I take something for the constipation?
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): More water for now. If it hasn't eased once we have the labs, we might add a stool softener. And don't restart the sertraline by yourself.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't. I've been doing these long days, though. That's the real problem, I think.
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): Long what? Say it again, this window popped up over your note.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Twelve-hour days. Four days a week. I'm a bookkeeper.
[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's a lot of hours. I'm not telling you to quit. I'll see you in two weeks to go over the bloodwork.
[SEG0073] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Only if she still feels bad?

[SEG0074] person_4 (DOCTOR): No, the two-week visit is happening either way, so we can look at the numbers. If something turns sharp before then — chest pain, you can't stay awake, constipation with vomiting — don't wait, call us or go to urgent care.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't have chest pain. The rest, I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0076] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. No chest pain. Nurse will draw the TSH, the free T4, and the CBC now. Water, vitamin D, no thyroid medicine.
[SEG0077] person_1 (NURSE): Come on, the chair's right down the hall. One quick stick.
[SEG0078] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. I still think it's the job. But... I don't know, doctor.

spec.situation: Middle-aged person tired and cold for months, weight up, constipated, low mood; pins it on work and age; mother had thyroid disease; one old thyroid test result recalled wrongly ('borderline, they said'). Blood test planned.
features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Weight gain supported, but onset 'last spring' was stated by husband, not patient.
bad.text: weight gain (category=constitutional, status=present, onset=last spring, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Patient denies allergies, but sulfa reaction is disputed in transcript.
Sertraline discontinued is supported; 50 mg dose is uncertain ('I think').
Transcript mentions an old thyroid test, but not that any thyroid blood test was completed in this encounter.

omissions.text: Low mood was further characterized: she does not cry and 'just doesn't care about stuff.'
Weight gain amount was specified by the patient as about 10 to 12 pounds, while the husband disputed that estimate and said the clothing size changed from size 8 to 12 since last spring.
Sleep symptom was more specific than 'sleeping too much': she sleeps 9 to 10 hours and is still wiped out.
Hair change was asked about and the patient was unsure ('maybe' but not sure).
Sertraline discontinuation timing was stated: she stopped it in March.
Reason for stopping sertraline was discussed: it made her feel flat, or she was already flat.
Past thyroid treatment history included that levothyroxine/thyroid hormone had been prescribed years ago but she never filled it and never took even one pill.

There was a real disagreement about the prior thyroid test result: the patient remembered being told it was 'borderline,' but her husband said Maple Street clinic told her it was normal; the doctor could not verify the outside record.

The recorded fact 'thyroid blood test (status=completed)' is misleading/wrong: the old thyroid test result was uncertain and unavailable in current records; today's thyroid labs were planned, not a confirmed completed prior result in chart.
An initial plan to start levothyroxine 25 micrograms daily and check TSH next week was proposed, then reversed after patient/family hesitation; final plan was no levothyroxine today.
The doctor specified the planned labs were not fasting.
The patient first denied allergies, then a possible sulfa reaction with lip swelling was documented because of the husband's report; the doctor explicitly noted the patient and husband do not agree.
Vitamin D adherence details were given: she takes it most days but forgets weekends, and the husband thought she misses more than that.
For constipation, the doctor advised more water now and said a stool softener might be added after labs if it has not eased.
The doctor said the two-week follow-up should occur regardless of whether she still feels bad, specifically to review the bloodwork.
Additional red-flag return precautions were given: call/go to urgent care for inability to stay awake or constipation with vomiting, in addition to chest pain.
A denied finding was explicitly obtained: the patient said she does not currently have chest pain.
